title: Collection of Biometric Data From Aliens Upon Entry to and Departure From the United States
summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a rule that allows U.S. Customs and Border Protection to photograph all non‑U.S. citizens when they enter or leave the country, and to collect other biometrics from non‑exempt travelers. It removes pilot limits so collection can happen at airports, seaports, land crossings, and other authorized departure points. The rule takes effect December 26, 2025, and DHS is asking for feedback now on how the new processes work at air entry, sea entry, and pedestrian land entry.

What this means in practice: officers take a quick live photo and compare it to images already on file from passports, visas, or past border crossings to verify identity. Fingerprints can still be used where needed. U.S. citizens can opt out of the photo step and be verified manually; if they do participate, their photos are deleted within 12 hours after citizenship is confirmed. Lawful permanent residents are treated as non‑citizens for this rule. The change also removes age‑based photo exemptions, so children and older adults who are not U.S. citizens may be photographed at entry and exit.

Who benefits: the government gains a stronger ability to confirm identities, spot imposters, reduce document fraud, and better track overstays—goals set by Congress after 9/11. Travelers may see faster lines where “face‑to‑document” checks replace scanning and manual lookups, and airlines and cruise lines may get more efficient boarding and debarkation. DHS says partners must purge images they collect on its behalf and comply with audits, encryption, and strict retention rules.

Who might be negatively affected: non‑U.S. citizens face broader biometric collection, including kids and seniors, which raises privacy concerns. Long‑term retention of alien photos in government systems also worries some. A small share of travelers may face added checks if their photo doesn’t match, which can mean short delays. Airlines, airports, and cruise lines that choose to participate will bear hardware and training costs. Pedestrians at land crossings may see slightly longer processing in some locations.

Money and timing: DHS estimates net costs in the hundreds of millions of dollars over 2017–2029, partly offset by time savings; security gains aren’t monetized. The system is already live at most air entries (Simplified Arrival), many air exits through airline partnerships, sea entries, and pedestrian land entries. DHS is still refining land vehicle lanes, sea exit, and private aircraft and will seek further public input as those roll out. Comments on the current collection processes are due November 26, 2025.
